articles.title: Kristaps Porzingis, Warriors Give Status Update as Health-Related Matter Sidelines Star Indefinitely
articles.summary: Kristaps Porzingis and the Golden State Warriors provided updates on the star's health status on Wednesday after he returned to the team's practice facility on Tuesday to meet with general manager Mike Dunleavy and vice president of player health and performance Rick Celebrini amid his ongoing absence from the team.
articles.body:
Kristaps Porzingis and the Golden State Warriors provided updates on the star's health status on Wednesday after he returned to the team's practice facility on Tuesday to meet with general manager Mike Dunleavy and vice president of player health and performance Rick Celebrini amid his ongoing absence from the team.

Porzingis said in a post on social media that he is "working with doctors and experts to figure out how to be fully back to good health asap." He added that the situation has "definitely been frustrating dealing with some health stuff that you can't exactly pinpoint."

The Warriors announced Wednesday that Porzingis will remain sidelined indefinitely due to a health-related matter but will be around the team moving forward. Golden State added it will provide an update on the veteran's status when available and appropriate.

Golden State Warriors head coach Steve Kerr told reporters last week that he hadn't seen Porzingis and added that it's "definitely concerning."

While Porzingis was out indefinitely to start training camp, general manager Mike Dunleavy Jr. told reporters last week that there was still a chance he'd start the season with the team.

"I'm not marking him down as being out to start the season or anything like that. He's just not available this week," he said.

Golden State opened training camp in Hawai'i before playing its first preseason game against the Los Angeles Clippers over the weekend in Honolulu. Porzingis did not travel with the team.

Porzingis has missed a combined 90 games over the past two seasons because of health issues. In February 2025, when he was with the Boston Celtics, he began experiencing a prolonged upper respiratory viral illness.

Ahead of the 2025-26 campaign, Porzingis revealed that he had been diagnosed with POTS, a disease that affects the autonomic nervous system and impacts the nerves that regulate blood flow, according to the Mayo Clinic . It causes symptoms like an overly rapid heartbeat and shortness of breath.

"It hit me, and it hit me like a truck," he told Fred Katz of The Athletic last October. "The breathing wasn't good. I did everything I could potentially to feel as good as I could, but my engine wasn't running the way I wanted."

Before his latest setback, Porzingis had been in the Warriors' facility taking part in offseason events.

"He's been participating in everything," Dunleavy said. "It just kind of popped up."

Porzingis, who joined the Warriors last year after being traded by the Atlanta Hawks, is an effective big man when available. He put up 16.7 points, 5.2 rebounds and 1.2 blocks per game across 32 contests last year.

Unfortunately for Porzingis, staying on the court consistently has been a struggle for him over the past few seasons.

articles.title: Baño del campeón Fenerbache a un flojo Valencia Basket (69-88)
articles.standfirst: La incombustible Meesseman (12+4+5) y Lacan (19) comandan la paliza turca a las taronjas, que tuvieron una puesta en escena nefasta (12-27)
articles.summary: La incombustible Meesseman (12+4+5) y Lacan (19) comandan la paliza turca a las taronjas, que tuvieron una puesta en escena nefasta (12-27)
articles.body: El Fenerbahce superó (69-88) este miércoles en el Roig Arena al Valencia Basket en la primera jornada de la fase de grupos de la Euroliga femenina, en un partido en el que dominó todos los aspectos del juego y en el que contó con la exterior Laia Lacan y la interior Emma Meesseman como referentes con 19 y 12 puntos, respectivamente. El Fenerbahce demostró su superioridad y su acierto en los primeros tres minutos de juego. A pesar del triple inicial de María Araújo, que le dio al Valencia Basket su única ventaja del partido, el equipo turco firmó un parcial de 3-9 de salida que obligó al técnico 'taronja' Javi Torralba a pedir tiempo muerto y a introducir a la base Leticia Romero en busca de un cambio de ritmo que no consiguió. Muy cómodo y muy superior físicamente tanto en defensa como en ataque, el Fenerbahce empezó a castigar la pintura local y a obtener segundas oportunidades que traducía en canastas y que estiraron la diferencia hasta los 15 puntos con la irrupción de Olcay Cakir (12-27, min.10). Los diez rebotes del equipo turco por los tres del valenciano y los 16 puntos en la pintura evidenciaban la fortaleza de las visitantes. El control del Fenerbahce se extendió en el segundo cuarto. Con la inspiración de Cakir y los puntos de Geiselsoder y Lacan llegó a ampliar su ventaja a los 17 puntos nada más comenzar. El Valencia Basket, que no era capaz de superar la defensa rival, tuvo en un triple de Alicia Flórez y en dos puntos de Alisia Jenkins la esperanza de engancharse al partido. Tanto, que el entrenador del Fenerbahce, Miguel Méndez, decidió parar el encuentro (24-37, min.15). Pero tras el tiempo muerto, el Fenerbahce volvió a pisar el acelerador. Un parcial de 0-11 elevó la distancia hasta los 24 puntos y noqueó de nuevo al Valencia Basket, que no encontraba la manera de frenar el vendaval ofensivo rival ni de cortar el ritmo de Lacan, la jugadora más inspirada del partido (30-50, min.20). La exterior francesa no bajó el pistón tras el descanso y con 5 puntos consecutivos mantuvo el alto listón de su equipo en los primeros compases de la segunda parte. Con el Fenerbahce dominando y el Valencia Basket yendo a remolque, el ritmo de juego decayó. Más todavía con la falta flagrante que sufrió la interior 'taronja' Elizabeth Balogun tras llevarse un duro golpe en la cara de Cakir. Bajo ese contexto, las visitantes cayeron en la relajación y el Valencia Basket trató de sacar el orgullo para rebajar la diferencia de veinte puntos con un parcial de 6-0 que obligó a pedir el segundo tiempo muerto de la noche a Méndez. Y como ocurrió en el primero, su equipo respondió. Juskaite y Geiselsolder castigaron una vez más bajo del aro y de nuevo la ventaja se ampliaba a los 20 puntos (46-66, min.28). La historia se repitió en el último cuarto. Un orgulloso Valencia Basket siguió remando hasta acercarse a los 14 puntos con un parcial de 7-0 que tejieron entre Balogun y Virag Takacs-Kiss (58-72, min.33). La solución del Fenerbahce fue otro tiempo de Méndez y otro castigo desde la pintura. Meesseman, Cakir y Lacan reactivaron el ataque de su equipo anotando tanto dentro como fuera y la distancia volvió a superar los 20 puntos. El parcial final llegó a ser de 4-16, aunque lo peor llegó en forma de lesión. La base Alexis Peterson tuvo que abandonar el partido acompañada por sus compañeras tras sufrir un golpe en la rodilla derecha en una acción con Alperi Onar con poco más de un minuto por jugar. La salida de Peterson, que no pudo apoyar la pierna hasta llegar al banquillo, terminó por enfriar un encuentro en el que el Valencia Basket no tuvo opciones reales de llevarse la victoria (69-88, min.40). 69 - Valencia Basket (12+18+21+18): Peterson (7), Pueyo (11), Balogun (9), Araújo (7), Borkowska (2) -cinco titular- Kiss (12), Broncano (-), Romero (2), Suárez (8), Bleda (-), Flórez (5), Jenkins (6). 88 - Fenerbahce (27+23+18+20): Allemand (3), Angloma (8), Lacan (19), Geiselsolder (9), Meesseman (12) -cinco titular- Anderson (7), Juskaite (8), Cakir (14), Onar (2), Gul (-), Pouye (-), Betts (6). Árbitros: Natasa Dragojevic, Bogna Podkowinska y Laure Coanus. Sin eliminadas. articles.title: Paliza de un Asisa Joventut coral a un flojo MoraBanc Andorra
articles.standfirst: Laprovittola (14+6+3), Reyes (17+5), Cheatham (14+5) y Ricky (5+3+12), brillan en la Penya
articles.summary: Laprovittola (14+6+3), Reyes (17+5), Cheatham (14+5) y Ricky (5+3+12), brillan en la Penya
articles.body: Al Asisa Joventut le bastaron los últimos 15 minutos de partido para doblegar al MoraBanc Andorra (96-75) y sumar el primer triunfo de la temporada en la Liga Endesa. Antes de arrancar el choque, los locales celebraron junto a la afición el título de la Supercopa Endesa ganado hace unas semanas. También se enseñó el nuevo banderín colgado en lo más alto del Olímpic de Badalona. Aunque ambos partidos tardaron en carburar en ataque, el Asisa Joventut fue el primero en tomar la delantera gracias a la dirección de juego formada por Ricky Rubio y Ludde Hakanson, que firmaron los primeros puntos de los suyos (10-5, min. 5). En un abrir y cerrar de ojos despertaron los andorranos con un inspiradísimo Wes Iwundu, que anotó seis puntos consecutivos para darle la vuelta al marcador y provocar el tiempo muerto de Dani Miret (10-13, min. 7). Desde entonces, intercambio de canastas que dejó al Asisa Joventut con un 23-22 al final del primer cuarto con los dos entrenadores descontentos por las defensas de sus equipos en el último tramo del periodo. La Penya puso la sexta marcha en el acelerador en el inicio del segundo cuarto, con un gran Emir Sulejmanovic en el juego interior, y pusieron hasta ocho puntos de renta en lo que fue la máxima en la primera mitad para los locales (33-25, min. 13). Un espejismo, ya que el MoraBanc Andorra respondió con un parcial similar y, tras varias jugadas positivas en ataque de Kassius Robertson, los visitantes igualaron el encuentro (37-37, min. 17). La buena dinámica de los del Principado se mantuvo e incluso lograron ponerse por delante con un 44-45, resultado con el que se llegó al tiempo de descanso. En la reanudación, volvieron los mejores minutos de Iwundu en el MoraBanc Andorra, aspecto que provocó un parcial favorable para ellos y poner su máxima, algo que metió el miedo en el cuerpo al público presente en el Olímpic (47-56, min. 24). Como era de esperar, el Asisa Joventut reaccionó y lo hizo de la mano de un Nico Laprovittola que no estuvo nada acertado anteriormente, pero cinco puntos prácticamente seguidos suyos dejó a su equipo a tan sólo tres puntos de desventaja (61-64, min. 28). En los últimos dos minutos del cuarto llegó el parcial badalonés con un acertado Kwan Cheatham desde la larga distancia, y los de Dani Miret se fueron con un 69-64 al final del tercer periodo, una ventaja clave teniendo en cuenta la igualdad del partido. La Penya mantuvo las buenas sensaciones del tramo final del cuarto anterior, y pese a los múltiples intentos de los visitantes de darle la vuelta al marcador, el acierto de Hakanson hizo que los suyos siguieran con una ligera ventaja en el luminoso (77-73, min. 33). Los badaloneses fueron a más y rápidamente se fueron más allá de los diez puntos de ventaja para dejar prácticamente sentenciado el choque tras unos buenos minutos del otro sueco, Simon Birgander, que fue de menos a más (89-73, min. 37). Al final, el Asisa Joventut venció por 96-75 al MoraBanc Andorra para sumar el primer triunfo de la temporada en la Liga Endesa, justo antes de recibir este domingo (19:00 horas) al Barça. 96. articles.title: Elle Duncan makes a fool of herself saying she and Black women are the real victims of the WNBA discourse
articles.summary: Elle Duncan calls WNBA discourse toxic and claims Black women are targeted, but her own career at ESPN and now Netflix tells a different story.
articles.body: Former ESPN anchor Elle Duncan called the discourse surrounding the WNBA "toxic as hell" and claimed that Black women are the target. "It feels like open season to dunk on Black women because we do not have protection. Because no one cares. Because we are low-hanging fruit," Duncan said of the WNBA discourse during a discussion with Front Office Sports on Tuesday. "It is very easy to dunk on us since we are, I would say, outside of transgender people, the most marginalized of the marginalized groups." FORMER ESPN ANCHOR SMEARS CAITLIN CLARK FANS WITH SWEEPING, FALSE ACCUSATIONS OF RACISM | MATT CALKINS Duncan, a highly peculiar individual, then accused "opportunists" of latching on to Caitlin Clark as a means of diminishing Black and queer women. "It’s twofold for them—so you get to lift this one person up, and you get to, ultimately, reduce everybody else that isn’t her to nothing," Duncan said. At this point, you probably expect us to respond to the examples Duncan provided to support her claims about Black women in America and the WNBA. Unfortunately, we cannot. Duncan didn't provide any. On the surface, I reject her premise. She says Black women lack protection, yet her own career suggests otherwise. ESPN hired Duncan after she was arrested for driving under the influence (DUI) in April 2013. She then repeatedly used ESPN's sports programming to make personal political statements. She reportedly lobbied behind the scenes to have the company remove Sage Steele from a social justice special in 2020 over concerns about Steele's "Blackness," whatever that means. Steele was removed. On at least two occasions, Duncan interrupted the network's sports coverage to protest legislation. She first called for a moment of silence in response to Florida's so-called "Don't Say Gay" bill. She later used the SportsCenter set to condemn the Supreme Court's decision to return abortion policy to the states, calling on fathers to support their daughters' ability to obtain abortions. Last year, she again ventured into political commentary on ESPN, declaring that "everyone" should adore and love former first lady Michelle Obama. Imagine the reaction if an ESPN anchor had instructed viewers that "everyone" should adore and love first lady Melania Trump. Yet ESPN did not discipline Duncan or distance itself from her commentary, as it did Steele after she discussed political and social issues in 2021. By that standard, Duncan appeared quite protected at ESPN. Despite all of that, Netflix has since hired her to anchor its sports coverage. Talk about privilege. I also reject the notion that Black women lack protection in the WNBA, a league composed predominantly of black women. Recently, A'ja Wilson charged aggressively toward a fan in the stands and avoided a suspension. DiJonai Carrington also avoided discipline after clotheslining Sophie Cunningham this summer and later accusing the WNBA of racism on social media from the locker room. Black women are also routinely afforded the benefit of the doubt by the media during WNBA controversies. ESPN's primary WNBA studio show features an all-black female panel and has often drawn criticism for holding Clark to a different standard than black players. Further, it's difficult to take Duncan seriously when she laments the toxicity surrounding WNBA coverage. Duncan was among the media figures who helped politicize the league when Clark arrived. She was initially ESPN's lead WNBA host, but was hardly a neutral observer. Duncan repeatedly shamed Clark over the supposed racism of anonymous online trolls, as if Clark were somehow responsible for them. She has continued to stoke the same divisions since joining Netflix. This summer, Duncan suggested Clark bore some responsibility for a wildly inappropriate USA Today column in which the author invoked Emmett Till while warning that Clark's silence in the face of online criticism could endanger black women. The racialization of the WNBA has never been particularly difficult to trace. Most people have been afraid to say where much of it originated. Clark is a straight White woman from Iowa who entered a predominantly black league with a level of fame no WNBA player had ever possessed. Players and media figures, many of whom were Black women, met her arrival with unmistakable resentment. Some explicitly attributed her popularity to white privilege. Others invoked the "great White hope" trope to explain her appeal. Elle Duncan, A'ja Wilson, DiJonai Carrington, Angel Reese, Monica McNutt, Cindy Brunson, Chiney Ogwumike, Sheryl Swoopes, and others are not innocent bystanders to the toxic WNBA discourse they now condemn. They have been among its most prominent participants. In many of the controversies that have defined the league's culture war, they have been the aggressors, not the targets. Duncan and others now want to reverse that sequence of events. They want the backlash against their own divisive rhetoric and behavior to serve as proof that black women were the victims all along. That's a convenient revision of what actually happened. WNBA discourse is "toxic as hell" in large part because a straight white woman from Iowa transcended the league, and too many people around the sport could not accept her success without filtering it through race, sexuality, and privilege. Rather than treat Clark's popularity as a historic opportunity for women's basketball, they treated it as a grievance. They framed her fame as "white privilege." They called her fans "racists" for defending her. Such dishonest framework guaranteed resentment. It also guaranteed backlash. Rinse and repeat. articles.title: Kristaps Porzingis Updates 'Frustrating' Health-Related Matter as Warriors Star Out Indefinitely
articles.summary: Golden State Warriors Kristaps Porziņģis provided an update on his health after the team said in a statement on Wednesday he would "remain out indefinitely" with the same "health-related matter" that has kept him out of training camp and the preseason.
articles.body:
Golden State Warriors Kristaps Porziņģis provided an update on his health after the team said in a statement on Wednesday he would "remain out indefinitely" with the same "health-related matter" that has kept him out of training camp and the preseason.

"Hello people, I'm working with doctors and experts to figure out how to be fully back to good health ASAP," the veteran big man wrote on social media . "Honestly, I'm getting better and better. I just have to stay patient, and I believe I'll be feeling great again soon. It has definitely been frustrating dealing with some health stuff that you can't exactly pinpoint, on top of injuries throughout my career, so it has added up for sure, but we will get through it. Health is wealth. Thank you for all the support. I appreciate all the Internet doctors trying to diagnose and help, but I'm in the best hands. So everyone can relax now, and I don't have HIV or AIDS."

Porzingis, 31, has played in just 74 games over the past two seasons, limited by postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS) that caused him to suffer an elevated heart rate and extreme fatigue.

"It hit me, and it hit me like a truck," Porziņģis told The Athletic's Fred Katz about the condition in Oct. 2025. "The breathing wasn't good. I did everything I could potentially to feel as good as I could, but my engine wasn't running the way I wanted. ... You know how people say, 'Oh, I'm so fatigued.' I've never used those words. I don't even like to speak in those terms, but I really was like that. At that time, I could just lay on the couch and be a house cat."

The Warriors acquired him last season ahead of February's trade deadline, though he appeared in just 17 games. When healthy he's been effective—for the Dubs, he averaged 16.1 points, 5.3 rebounds, 2.3 assists and 1.1 blocks per game. In theory he's a logical fit next to Draymond Green in the team's frontcourt, providing floor spacing on offense and rim protection on defense.

But given the uncertainty surrounding Porziņģis' health condition, it's unclear when—or how often—he'll see the court for Golden State. With Jimmy Butler also sidelined to start the season as he recovers from a torn ACL, the Warriors are going to be shorthanded.

articles.title: WNBA Finals Ticket Prices Reach Historic Levels for Angel Reese, Dream vs. Valkyries at Hawks' Arena
articles.summary: Ticket prices for the 2026 WNBA Finals between the Atlanta Dream and Golden State Valkyries have climbed to historic levels.
articles.body:
Ticket prices for the 2026 WNBA Finals between the Atlanta Dream and Golden State Valkyries have climbed to historic levels.

Game 3 in Atlanta currently contains a get-in price of $201, representing the most expensive WNBA Finals game on record (via TickPick ).

The Valkyries are hosting the first two games of the series before Angel Reese and the Dream will return home for the next pair of contests.

Games 3 and 4 of the Finals are set to be played at State Farm Arena, which is usually home to the Atlanta Hawks.

The Dream typically host games at Gateway Center Arena, but the WNBA announced that the team would move to State Farm Arena for the upcoming series on Tuesday.

Gateway Center Arena has a capacity of just 3,500, while State Farm Arena can hold over 17,000 fans.

The Dream are looking to capture their first championship in franchise history, compiling a 30-14 record in the regular season before sweeping the first two rounds of the playoffs.

Reese has been a key piece of Atlanta's two-way success, averaging a career-high 16.4 points to go along with 12.1 rebounds, 2.8 assists and 1.8 steals per game. She was named Defensive Player of the Year for the 2026 season on Oct. 1.

As for the Valkyries, they posted a 32-12 regular-season record as well as a 5-1 mark in the playoffs. Golden State's dominance has been particularly impressive considering the organization joined the WNBA as an expansion team in 2025.

Game 1 between the Dream and Valkyries begins on Saturday at 3:30 p.m. ET.

Apoteósico inicio de La Laguna Tenerife en su vuelta al Santiago Martín, en el que sus jugadores completaron un sobresaliente primer cuarto en el que mostraron un gran acierto tanto en la parcela ofensiva como en la defensiva, con dos parciales de 7-0 prácticamente consecutivos que desesperaron a los italianos e influyeron notablemente en su acierto en el tiro, con tan solo cinco puntos anotados tras los primeros siete minutos (18-5). articles.body: El Recoletas Salud San Pablo Burgos cayó en casa ante el Hapoel Jerusalén (81-83) en la tercera jornada de la Eurocopa de baloncesto, en un partido en el que fue a remolque durante buena parte del encuentro, pero en el que rozó la remontada en un último cuarto de máxima igualdad. Los de Porfi Fisac llegaron a ponerse por delante, aunque no aprovecharon sus últimas tres oportunidades de canasta para forzar la victoria. El equipo burgalés arrancó con energía y encontró en Taboada a su principal referencia ofensiva, con sus primeras acciones permitieron a los locales tomar la iniciativa en el marcador, con el apoyo de Audige y Doumbouya. El San Pablo llegó a disfrutar de una ventaja que obligó a Sasa Obradovic a detener el partido con un tiempo muerto, sin embargo, el Hapoel fue encontrando soluciones a través de Lofton y Miletic, antes de cerrar el primer cuarto por delante (18-24), después de un parcial favorable que cambió la dinámica inicial. El segundo periodo confirmó las dificultades de los de Porfi Fisac para frenar el ataque visitante. Levi y Cacok ampliaron la renta israelí, mientras Smith y Lofton castigaban a la defensa burgalesa y una técnica señalada a Porfi Fisac llegó con el marcador en 22-35, en un tramo complicado para los locales. El San Pablo trató de mantenerse en el partido con el acierto de Steward, Doumbouya y Sengfelder, mientras que Radosavljevic también aportó puntos importantes, pero el Hapoel conservó el control y alcanzó el descanso con siete puntos de margen, tras la reacción final burgalesa. Los burgaleses salieron con otra energía tras el descanso y encontraron en Doumbouya y Radosavljevic las primeras respuestas ofensivas. Audige y Sengfelder, este último especialmente inspirado, lideraron la remontada local hasta igualar el marcador (52-52) y Samar culminó la reacción al situar al San Pablo por delante (55-54), lo que obligó al Hapoel a recuperar su mejor versión. La respuesta visitante llegó de la mano de Zoosman y Lofton, que devolvieron la iniciativa a los israelíes mientras que San Pablo perdió fluidez ofensiva en el tramo final del cuarto y el Hapoel aprovechó la situación para abrir brecha (57-70). Doumbouya recortó distancias desde la línea de tiros libres, pero los burgaleses afrontaron el último periodo con la obligación de remontar de nuevo. Taboada y Steward encabezaron la reacción burgalesa para reducir la diferencia hasta los dos puntos (66-68), mientras el equipo de Porfi Fisac elevaba la intensidad y encontraba mejores soluciones en ataque. Taboada mantuvo a los locales en la pelea y Dani Díez y Samar prolongaron la remontada hasta situar el marcador en 74-75. El San Pablo no se rindió. Doumbouya y Radosavljevic volvieron a acercar a los burgaleses y una canasta de Dani Díez puso por delante a los locales (79-78). Sin embargo, Lofton devolvió la ventaja al Hapoel y Steward respondió para establecer el 81-80. Con 43 segundos por jugarse, Milton anotó para colocar el 81-83. El conjunto burgalés dispuso después de tres oportunidades consecutivas para igualar o ponerse por delante, pero no consiguió convertir ninguna de ellas y dejó escapar sus opciones de culminar la remontada. Roddy metió la canasta de la victoria y con 1 segundo por jugarse Taboada anoto el triple para poner el 84-85 definitivo. 84 - San Pablo Burgos (18+21+20+25): Chase Audige (4), Ziga Samar (5), Balsa Koprivica (0), Sekou Doumbouya (15), Joaquín Taboada (20) -cinco inicial- DJ Steward (11), Pablo Almazán (0), Dani Díez (4), Rubén Guerrero (0), Dusan Radosavljevic (8), Christian Sengfelder (15), Raúl Lobaco (2). 85 - Hapoel Midtown Jerusalem (24+22+24+15): Kenny Lofton Jr. (28), Lorenzo Brown (0), Dusan Miletic (4), David Roddy (8), Ethan Burg (3) -cinco inicial- Davonte Cacok (11), Jaleen Smith (13), Yotam Hanochi (-), Shake Milton (7), Roi Huber (-), Nimrod Levi (6), Yovel Zoosman (5). articles.title: Kristaps Porziņģis is 'getting better and better,' but Warriors say he will remain out indefinitely due to 'health-related matter'
articles.summary: It's still unclear what exactly Porziņģis is dealing with, a week away from Golden State's regular-season opener.
articles.body:
The Kristaps Porziņģis mystery continued on Wednesday when the Golden State Warriors announced that the 31-year-old Latvian frontcourt standout will remain out indefinitely due to a "health-related matter" but will be around the team.

It's still unclear what exactly Porziņģis is dealing with, a week away from Golden State's regular-season opener in Los Angeles against the Lakers.

"Hello people, I'm working with doctors and experts to figure out how to be fully back to good health asap," the one-time All-Star and NBA champion wrote . "Honestly, I'm getting better and better. I just have to stay patient, and I believe I'll be feeling great again soon. "It has definitely been frustrating dealing with some health stuff that you can't exactly pinpoint, on top of injuries throughout my career, so it has added up for sure, but we will get through it. "Health is wealth. Thank you for all the support."

In a reply to that message on X, Porziņģis also said:

"I appreciate all the internet doctors trying to diagnose and help, but I'm in the best hands. So everyone can relax now … and I don't have hiv or aids."

The Warriors explained that Porziņģis, who missed training camp and the team's first five preseason games, returned to Golden State's practice facility on Tuesday. There, he met with general manager Mike Dunleavy and Dr. Rick Celebrini, the Warriors' vice president of player health and performance.

"The specific contents of that meeting will remain private," the organization's release read.

It also noted: "An update on his status, including the potential resumption of practice, playing status or timeline, will be provided when available and appropriate."

While the nature of whatever issue Porziņģis is navigating hasn't been disclosed, him breaking his silence on the matter is notable.

As Porziņģis alluded to in his online comments on Wednesday, he's faced several obstacles during a 10-season NBA career, which he began with the New York Knicks (2015-19) before spending time with the Dallas Mavericks (2019-22), Washington Wizards (2022-23), Boston Celtics (2023-25), Hawks (2025-26) and now the Warriors.

Chief among Porziņģis' setbacks was postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS) , a non-life-threatening condition, according to the Cleveland Clinic , "that causes a number of symptoms when you transition from lying down to standing up, such as a fast heart rate, dizziness and fatigue." POTS significantly limited the 7-foot-2 Porziņģis during an Eastern Conference semifinals series against the Knicks amid the 2024-25 campaign.

Porziņģis averaged a mere 15.5 minutes in that six-game series, in which Boston's NBA title defense came to an end, with Celtics head coach Joe Mazzulla revealing after Game 5 that Porziņģis didn't play in the second half that day because " he couldn't breathe ."

Last season, Porziņģis appeared in only 32 games: 17 for the Hawks and 15 for the Warriors. Illness sidelined him while he was with the Hawks, too .

He was dealt to Golden State in an exchange that landed Atlanta Jonathan Kuminga and Buddy Hield. Back then, Porziņģis was nursing an Achilles injury.

Last season, during an appearance on 95.7 The Game, longtime Warriors head coach Steve Kerr was asked about Porziņģis' POTS struggles, and Kerr infamously referred to Porziņģis' diagnosis as "misinformation." A day later, Kerr apologized for what he called "a stupid mistake."

"I regretted even trying to discuss the diagnosis," Kerr said back then, in late February. "That was my mistake. I need to leave that to professionals."

Despite the availability concerns surrounding Porziņģis, the Warriors signed him to a two-year extension reportedly worth $40 million this past offseason . That said, per ESPN , only $3 million of the $20 million next season is guaranteed. When healthy, Porziņģis — who helped the Celtics win it all in 2024 — is still productive on the court.

Staying on the court has been the challenge for him, particularly of late.

articles.title: Ex-SJSU volleyball coach files new lawsuit alleging retaliation for Trump support, religion amid trans scandal
articles.summary: Melissa Batie-Smoose's new federal lawsuit alleges Todd Kress mocked her Trump support and religious beliefs before SJSU stripped her duties.
articles.body: EXCLUSIVE: Former San Jose State University volleyball assistant coach has filed a new lawsuit over her alleged treatment during and before the school's scandal involving transgender athlete Blaire Fleming and female teammate Brooke Slusser. Melissa Batie-Smoose filed an initial lawsuit last October, but it was dismissed in September. But she's not backing down, and is now making new allegations about what happened before she was suspended and eventually let go from her position. Her new complaint alleges that SJSU head volleyball coach Todd Kress mocked her for supporting Donald Trump in front of players, reacted with hostility to her religious objections to a transgender athlete’s participation, and made her feel "physically unsafe" during certain interactions. The complaint alleges she repeatedly told Kress, "in substance," that "God made man and woman" and that her beliefs prevented her from treating a male athlete as female. She claims Kress responded with hostility toward those beliefs and disparaged her politics. CAMPUS CONFLICT EXPOSED AT THE CORE OF SJSU'S MESSY FIGHT VS TRUMP ADMIN OVER VOLLEYBALL SCANDAL "Kress would also berate her during practice in front of the athletes, calling her ‘Trump-loving’ or a ‘Trump lover’ and mocking her political affiliation," the complaint states. Elsewhere, the filing alleges that Kress knew she was a Republican who had voted for Trump and used those remarks to damage her relationship with players, excluded her from meetings and reduced coaching duties. The relationship at the center of the new complaint began well before the controversy. Batie-Smoose says she worked with Kress at Florida State in 2006 and again at Fairfield University from 2019 through 2022. When Kress moved to San Jose State, she accepted the associate head coaching position and relocated her family from Connecticut to California in January 2023. Batie-Smoose has previously alleged she learned that Fleming was transgender only after arriving in 2023. Over the next two seasons, Batie-Smoose says, disagreements about Fleming’s participation became entangled with her relationship with Kress, her responsibilities on the court and her standing inside the athletic department. One alleged confrontation described in the complaint began with a canceled recruiting visit. In approximately August 2023, a hurricane disrupted a recruit’s flight. Batie-Smoose says she returned from the airport to the gym to update Kress, who ignored her greeting twice. After she commented on his behavior, she alleges, he followed her into her office and closed the door. The complaint says he "cornered, yelled at, and berated her" and told her he could get her fired. Batie-Smoose describes feeling physically unsafe during the encounter. She says she reported the incident to athletics human resources and an administrator overseeing the program, but "in response, Plaintiff was told that Kress was her boss and that she needed to listen to him. Kress received no disciplinary action for his behavior towards Plaintiff." The filing also describes alleged confrontations involving players. OutKick is not disclosing the names of the players. The complaint alleges Kress berated one athlete "so harshly for not passing her running test that she experienced panic attacks. Plaintiff reported this mistreatment to Alexander. Upon information and belief, Kress was not disciplined." It described another alleged incident in which a player was "excoriated by Kress in front of the team for being a few minutes late to the locker room after a losing match. The ferocity of his interaction resulted in both Plaintiff and [the player] informing Alexander about the incident. Upon information and belief, Kress was not disciplined." The new complaint also separately cites an older accusation against Kress. Fox News Digital reported in July that a former Fairfield player had accused Kress of a 1998 hotel-room assault. Batie-Smoose’s filing alleges that the former player notified SJSU in October 2024 and that an official acknowledged her stated safety concern. It argues that the university’s handling of that report supports her claim of disparate treatment. "Plaintiff is further informed and believes, based on public reporting, that Defendant took no further action following this correspondence, and that Kress continued to coach and travel with the SJSU women’s volleyball team without interruption or restriction. Plaintiff alleges that Defendant’s handling of this report is consistent with, and corroborates, the pattern of disparate treatment against Plaintiff alleged throughout this Complaint," the lawsuit states. On Oct. 29, 2024, Batie-Smoose submitted a Title IX complaint alleging unequal treatment and failures to address concerns inside the program regarding the transgender athlete and the female players on that year's team. Days later, the university placed her on paid administrative leave. According to her new lawsuit, her punishment arrived on Nov. 2, about 90 minutes before a home match: a university administrator blocked her entry to the gym, required her to surrender her identification and keys, and instructed her to leave. She alleges she could not retrieve belongings from her office. The filing includes an attachment of her suspension letter. The letter referenced a complaint against Batie-Smoose dated Oct. 24 — five days before her own Title IX submission. The allegations included differential treatment based on a protected status, disclosure of confidential student information, drinking with athletes during team travel, unprofessional or insubordinate conduct, inappropriate language and a failure or refusal to coach athletes. The letter prohibited campus access and contact with student-athletes and imposed restrictions on discussing the investigation, with exceptions including legal counsel and a union representative. Batie-Smoose alleges the university used the accusations as a pretext and enforced its rules differently against her than against Kress. She denies improperly disclosing protected education records and says the information she discussed came from public sources or personal observations. Batie-Smoose acknowledged having a drink in an airport lounge while adult players were present, but says she neither purchased their drinks nor encouraged them to drink. She alleges another male coach was drinking there without facing the same consequences. She also denies directing inappropriate language at players or refusing to coach an athlete for whom she had responsibility. On Jan. 31, 2025, athletics director Jeff Konya notified her that her temporary coaching appointment would not be renewed, in a letter issued on behalf of President Cynthia Teniente-Matson. Batie-Smoose's latest lawsuit was filed Oct. 13 in the Northern District of California, the lawsuit names the California State University trustees and 11 university employees, including Kress, after a legal setback in September. On Sept. 4, Judge Noël Wise dismissed Batie-Smoose’s previous amended complaint, which asserted discrimination and retaliation under Title VII and Title IX. Wise found that the allegations did not plausibly connect the suspension or nonrenewal to Batie-Smoose’s sex or protected advocacy. The order emphasized the complaint’s account that the university acted after she disclosed student information to the media despite instructions to keep it confidential. "Plaintiff’s complaint supports that she was disciplined for violating a confidentiality law, not for opposing discrimination on the basis of sex," Wise wrote. The ruling granted leave to amend within 21 days, so now Batie-Smoose and her attorneys have escalated their fight with a trove of new allegations. SJSU and CSU have declined to provide responses to Batie-Smoose's latest complaint. INSIDE THE FALLOUT OF THE SJSU VOLLEYBALL SCANDAL: ‘THIS IS AN OBVIOUS PROBLEM’ "Due to pending litigation, San Jose State is unable to comment," an SJSU spokesperson told OutKick. A CSU spokesperson responded, writing, "The CSU is not commenting at this time. We were made aware of the lawsuit yesterday and are still reviewing the claims." The new complaint comes as SJSU and CSU find themselves in the midst of a mult-front legal battle with Batie-Smoose, former athletes, and President Donald Trump's administration over the scandal. On Jan. 28, 2026, the Education Department’s Office for Civil Rights issued a findings letter addressing SJSU’s volleyball program. The letter, attached to Batie-Smoose’s new complaint, concluded that the university violated Title IX in its treatment of athletic participation, sex-separated facilities and the handling of discrimination complaints. On employment and scholarships, the letter expressed compliance concerns and identified evidence it considered indicative of unequal treatment, while acknowledging gaps in the records. Some of the most consequential passages concern the university’s handling of its two coaches. OCR reported that personnel investigations involving Batie-Smoose and Kress were opened on Nov. 12, 2024, and questioned why the university suspended her but not him. The letter cited investigator notes stating that Kress "crossed the FERPA line in his interview with ESPN," referring to the federal student privacy law. The letter also described internal records suggesting officials worried that suspending Kress could "spark more media attention" and "unduly disrupt the team." The lawsuit, citing those passages, argues that privacy and team stability were applied selectively. CSU disputes that comparison. Its March complaint against the Education Department argues that the coaches were not similarly situated, that Batie-Smoose disclosed protected information, and that an investigation found insufficient evidence that Kress retaliated against Slusser. The system also challenges the federal investigation’s procedures and conclusions. Meanwhile, CSU’s disagreement with Washington has become a lawsuit of its own. The university system sued the Education Department on March 6, arguing that the government was attempting to punish SJSU retroactively for conduct consistent with the law, federal guidance and NCAA rules in effect during the 2022–24 seasons. CSU declined the federal government’s proposed resolution agreement. It maintains that protecting transgender students and complying with then-governing rules did not amount to unlawful sex discrimination. Federal officials threatened enforcement that could put funding at risk. But a March 31 court order established protections against funding disruption based on the challenged findings. The legal landscape has also changed since the 2024 season. On Feb. 6, 2025, the NCAA changed its policy to restrict competition on women’s teams to athletes assigned female at birth, following Trump’s executive order the previous day. The policy permits athletes assigned male at birth to practice with women’s teams under specified conditions. On June 30, 2026, the Supreme Court upheld the challenged restrictions in West Virginia and Idaho, ruling that Title IX and the Equal Protection Clause permit schools to reserve female teams based on biological sex. The court expressly left unresolved a separate question: whether schools may allow transgender women and girls to participate on female teams. That limitation matters in the SJSU dispute, where permission to exclude and a legal obligation to exclude are different issues. In March, a Colorado federal judge dismissed the Mountain West defendants from the lawsuit brought by Slusser, Batie-Smoose and other volleyball players. The court found that the conference was not subject to Title IX and was not a state actor for the constitutional claims. It also dismissed several claims against university officials, while deferring a ruling on Title IX damages claims against the CSU trustees pending the Supreme Court’s decision. Supplemental briefing continued after that decision. For Batie-Smoose, the latest suit seeks both compensation and restoration of her professional standing. She requests reinstatement to her former job or a comparable position, back pay and other compensatory relief, punitive damages against individually liable defendants, legal fees and a jury trial. She also asks for removal or correction of adverse personnel records, including the suspension letter, the later evaluation and an October 2025 nondiscrimination-policy finding. The complaint specifies no total damages figure. She has returned to coaching elsewhere. Cisco College announced her appointment as head volleyball coach in April. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP But her new filing asks a court to revisit the place she left: the gym entrance where she says her work was interrupted, the personnel file that followed, and the university decisions that she alleges converted a dispute over women’s sports into the loss of her job. CSU has disputed the broader accusations against SJSU. In its own litigation against the Department of Education, the university system says it followed the law and athletic eligibility rules applicable during the seasons at issue, protected student privacy and investigated complaints. It also says an investigation found that Batie-Smoose discriminated against Blaire Fleming because of sex and gender identity. Batie-Smoose contests the university’s findings and denies refusing to coach any athlete.

articles.title: ESPN Legend Urges Indiana Fever to Pursue UCLA Coach Cori Close if Stephanie White Replaced
articles.summary: Stephanie White’s future with the Indiana Fever has been a topic of discussion among fans following the team’s first-round playoff exit. Given how poorly the...
articles.body:
Stephanie White's future with the Indiana Fever has been a topic of discussion among fans following the team's first-round playoff exit. Given how poorly the season went for Indiana, it was hardly surprising that White emerged as one of the top candidates on the hot seat for much of the 2026 season.

There has been plenty of speculation about potential replacements. While the franchise has yet to make any announcements, fans and pundits continue to discuss possible candidates as the Fever consider their options.

Former ESPN star Linda Cohn is among those who have a name in mind that could be a great fit for Caitlin Clark and the team. On her YouTube channel on Wednesday, Cohn shared that UCLA coach Cori Close is the candidate who intrigues her most for the Fever job.

"Big fan I am of Cori Close, the head coach of the UCLA Bruins. And when you look at what she has accomplished, particularly when it comes to developing players and building a championship program, a winning culture, there's a lot to like from Cori Close," Cohn said (Timestamp: 2:00).

Cohn pointed to how Close built the UCLA program and helped six Bruins players get selected in the 2026 WNBA draft, setting a record for the most players drafted from one program.

"Impressive resume. That doesn't happen by accident, by the way. That takes work. There's something genuine there. That tells me something about her: her ability to identify talent, develop that talent, bring different personalities together — I like that one — and prepare players for the next level. And isn't that exactly what Indiana needs? … And if I'm running the Fever, that is a phone call I'm picking up the phone to make, because Cori Close checks so many boxes when it comes to developing players, building a program, creating a winning culture. She would be my first choice right now."

Given Close's success at UCLA, a WNBA team may look to follow a similar approach by hiring a coach with a proven track record of building a winning program, despite having no prior WNBA coaching experience. Close has said that she may consider a move to the WNBA someday . With that in mind, the possibility of Close making the jump to the WNBA should not be ruled out.

Linda Cohn Points Out a Pathway for Cori Close to Land the WNBA Job

Cori Close signed a four-year, $8.0375 million contract extension in May. However, the contract includes a provision specifically addressing a potential move to become a WNBA head coach, significantly reducing the buyout.

Linda Cohn cited Front Office Sports , noting that if Close leaves UCLA to become a WNBA head coach, the buyout would be just 25% of the normal amount. If she leaves before the end of March 2027, the buyout would be approximately $500,000. Starting in April 2027, it would drop to around $437,000.

"Now, we're talking about a coach who just signed a contract worth more than $8 million. So, clearly there is a pathway. I found a pathway for her to make the jump to the WNBA without an enormous financial penalty. And if I'm the Indiana Fever, I'm (Fever general manager) Amber Cox, that's something I'm paying very close attention to," Cohn said.

As impressive as Close's resume is, it's hard to imagine how things could work out better for her and the Fever. If Indiana decides the best path forward is to retool and get back into championship contention, Close could be the right choice.

While the move feels more like a long shot, it's certainly something to watch during the offseason. Close has the potential to be a good hire for the Fever, but time will tell if she ends up being their next head coach.

articles.title: Caleb Wilson's Final Box Score Stats, Highlights from Bulls vs. Bucks Preseason
articles.summary: After impressing through his first three preseason games, Chicago Bulls rookie Caleb Wilson struggled a bit in a win over the Milwaukee Bucks.
articles.body:
After impressing through his first three preseason games, Chicago Bulls rookie Caleb Wilson struggled a bit in a win over the Milwaukee Bucks.

The No. 4 overall pick out of North Carolina couldn't get his shot to fall and wasn't able to take care of the ball against the Bucks.

While he couldn't get much going on offense, he still put together a solid highlight package.

Wednesday marked Wilson's worst game of the preseason so far, but it was by no means an awful showing from the young player. He's still getting comfortable against NBA talent, and there are bound to be some nights when his shot isn't falling.

Wilson has been otherwise strong so far, dropping 15, 21 and 17 points in his first three games.

The Bulls are still in rebuild mode at this point, but if Wilson pans out the way they hope, he could expedite that rebuild substantially. The first step, though, is getting him adjusted to the league.

Preseason helped Wilson gain his footing, but the real thing starts next week. Wilson will make his NBA debut next Wednesday against the Toronto Raptors.

articles.title: Jalen Brunson-Inspired Discount Coming to NYC Restaurant Ahead of Knicks' Title Defense Season
articles.summary: Jalen Brunson and the New York Knicks will begin their title defense campaign next week against the Philadelphia 76ers, and a local restaurant is running a special promotion to welcome the new season.
articles.body:
Jalen Brunson and the New York Knicks will begin their title defense campaign next week against the Philadelphia 76ers, and a local restaurant is running a special promotion to welcome the new season.

Sei Less, an Asian-fusion restaurant in midtown Manhattan, is offering fans 11 percent off their bill if they come in wearing Knicks gear on Oct. 20, when New York opens its season against the Sixers, per TMZ .

The discount is, of course, a reference to Brunson's jersey number.

"It's only right as a diehard Knicks fan that we give back for all the pain and suffering over the last 53 years," Sei Less owner Dara Mirjahangiry said, per TMZ. "We're four blocks from Madison Square Garden, our proximity, we're the hotspot for Knicks fans before and after games, and we take care of a lot of the current and former players. So it's just a small give back we could do for all the fans in the area."

TMZ noted that several past and current Knicks have eaten at Sei Less, including Carmelo Anthony, Amar'e Stoudemire and Karl-Anthony Towns.

Sei Less is ensuring fans are fed on game day, and it's up to Brunson and the Knicks to deliver a win to start the season.

articles.title: Amar'e Stoudemire Graduates from Police Academy, NBA Hall of Famer to Serve Miami-Dade Schools PD
articles.summary: NBA Hall of Famer Amar'e Stoudemire graduated from the Miami Dade College School of Justice's Basic Law Enforcement Academy on Wednesday.
articles.body:
NBA Hall of Famer Amar'e Stoudemire graduated from the Miami Dade College School of Justice's Basic Law Enforcement Academy on Wednesday.

According to the school, "For Amar'e, this is more than a second career. Becoming a police officer was a childhood dream, inspired in part by family members who served in law enforcement. Now, he will begin a new chapter as a police officer with the Miami Dade Schools Police Department, giving back to our community and serving as a positive influence for the next generation."

Stoudemire, 43, played for the Phoenix Suns, New York Knicks, Dallas Mavericks and Miami Heat in his 14-season NBA career, last appearing during the 2015-16 season. He was a six-time All-Star and five-time All-NBA selection, averaging 21.9 points, 9.1 rebounds and 1.4 blocks per game in his career.

articles.title: How Pete Sousa’s Road to Sobriety Led Him Back to a Sports Media Career He Thought He Lost
articles.summary: "When you get sober, the sky is the limit. I'm living, breathing proof of that. People thought I was extremely hopeless. I'm here to tell anyone with a probl...
articles.body:
In any lifetime, mistakes happen. They are always forgivable, but only if one has the courage to admit them. Pete Sousa is no different from anyone else. At one point, he was a rising star in sports media. After a career in NBA public relations, he worked for the Philadelphia 76ers and Charlotte Bobcats for almost a decade. But Sousa was dealing with his own personal demons tied to addiction, a common trait on his father's side of the family.

"When I was working in Charlotte to work on radio, I was in bad shape. I was a real alcohol and drug addict, and I brought some of that to work for me. I was not my best self," explained Sousa, who spent one season with Charlotte. "Day in the day, I used to lament that I let these opportunities slip through my fingertips. But all of that had to happen for me to get sober."

Sousa's media career was flourishing in his younger days. It's rare for someone to pivot from the communications world and take a leap of faith into play-by-play. That's the journey Sousa took, shifting from years of experience in media relations to becoming an on-air presence himself.

But his struggles with addiction put a pause on his growth in sports media.

"When I was in Charlotte, I was reading this book called 'Moments of Clarity.' It's a collection of notable people who shared their stories of sobriety. The book was so relatable, I figured, if they could do it, why can't I?" said Sousa.

After wrapping up the season in 2015, Sousa checked himself into rehab for 30 days. After completing treatment, he moved into a halfway house and earned a job at Kentucky Fried Chicken. This came after a promising career in sports media and professional sports, and it was obviously a far cry from where he envisioned himself.

"I really bottomed out and had that gift of desperation. But getting sober came together at the right time," said Sousa. "When I got sober, I identified what I was going to do. Take the steps to do it and fail. I just went out from working in the NBA to Kentucky Fried Chicken. I endured a shitload of rejection but kept going."

The work began again for Sousa. He landed a play-by-play role in the NBA Development League and eventually made a short return to Charlotte, working radio for Hornets games. He then pivoted again to local television news in Louisiana and Texas for the next nine years while rebuilding his play-by-play profile, calling college football, baseball and basketball for ESPN, primarily covering the Big 12.

Last month, Sousa added another element to his arsenal when he was named the new co-host of The Drake Toll Show on Westwood One Sports.

"Over the summer, I filled in for Westwood One to get a vibe check for the executives with Westwood One Sports. Armen Williams arranged for me to do some fill-in work previously, so I was on the radar," noted Sousa. "I've known Drake [Toll] from years ago, and always thought Drake was a superstar."

Sousa's relationship with Toll dates back to when both worked in Waco, Texas, albeit not together. Over time, they developed a mutual respect for one another as Sousa called play-by-play and Toll began building his multimedia brand.

When Westwood One Sports was beginning to take shape, Toll encouraged network management to take a look at Sousa for potential work with the new network. While the two sides didn't come to an agreement at the onset, Williams kept Sousa on standby for fill-in work over the summer.

"I told Armen [Williams] I would always love to fill in because terrestrial radio was always something I wanted to do. I was raised on Howard Stern and Howard Eskin, and thought radio was the coolest medium. It meant something to me," said Sousa. "I do a lot of play-by-play, and I can have a colorful personality. But there's only so far you can go."

Sousa admits that while he always had plenty of opinions on sports, he never took any of them seriously. Because of his experience playing, observing and seeing what goes into any role in collegiate or professional sports, he didn't consider himself at a level where he could confidently express those opinions.

Instead, the support system around him, from personal friends to colleagues in the industry, helped build his confidence and encouraged him to begin expressing himself. He formed a podcast called The Pete Sousa Show , where he began sharing his opinions and analysis on everything happening in sports. His experience working in public relations also provided a prerequisite understanding of how an opinion can feel on the other side.

"When you show up to an arena and see the sports information guy, I have a ton of respect for those guys. I also understand how players are disappointed after being roasted by the media. I've seen it firsthand and how it affects them," explained Sousa. "The human experience is what I'm in touch with, and I feel people respect that about me. I'm more about explaining why instead of shooting from the hip."

When it comes to opportunities, Sousa has learned never to turn down a chance to learn. He credits his time as a news anchor with helping him battle through his dyslexia while working with a live teleprompter. It was another example of working through a struggle to develop an additional skill in his arsenal.

His journey to sobriety also gave him a new appreciation for every opportunity. Knowing full well that nothing is guaranteed, Sousa makes the most of each one.

"With me, a lot of it is fear because I worked so hard to get here. Getting sober. Living in a halfway house. I've done some terrible jobs, but it was about doing whatever I needed to do to get here," said Sousa. "I don't say no because I'm scared people will stop asking. I'm so fortunate to get so many opportunities. You always have to think that anyone could be watching or listening."

Now on the other side of his journey to sobriety, Sousa enjoys every opportunity to share his story. In hopes it can provide comfort or confidence for others. He plans to relaunch his Payoff with Pete Sousa podcast , which showcases the stories of others and their journeys as well.

Understanding that every journey is different for those dealing with addiction, Sousa hopes his positivity, authenticity and perspective can provide hope through his example.

"There's always hope. Life can be short," said Sousa. "When you get sober, the sky is the limit. I'm living, breathing proof of that. People thought I was extremely hopeless. I'm here to tell anyone with a problem, if you think you're hopeless, that is not true. If you go through the right process with the right people, you don't have to do this alone."

For Sousa, the journey is no longer about making up for the opportunities he believes he lost. It's about appreciating the ones he has today and understanding that every stop along the way helped shape the person and broadcaster he has become.

The road from professional sports to a halfway house and a job at Kentucky Fried Chicken was not the career path Sousa envisioned. But it gave him something far more valuable than another line on a resume. It gave him perspective, and humility. Plus, an understanding of what it means to keep moving forward when the next step isn't always obvious.

Today, Sousa is still building his career across play-by-play, radio, television and podcasting. But his most important work may be what happens when the microphone is turned toward his own story. By being open about addiction, recovery, rejection and the long road back, he has given others a reason to believe their own story doesn't have to end at its lowest point.

Sousa knows there will always be another challenge, another opportunity and another chance to learn. After everything he's experienced, he no longer takes any of them for granted. He simply keeps showing up, keeps saying yes and keeps moving forward.

"I want to continue to evolve and give back to the people who provided me opportunities," said Sousa. "I know what it's like to go to a job that you don't love, and I want people to laugh and enjoy life. That's what I hope my work with The Drake Toll Show provides. Honestly, I'm waiting for someone to knock on my door and say this is a mistake… I have a great level of gratitude for these chances I've been given."

If Pete Sousa's journey has taught him anything, it's that hitting bottom doesn't have to be the end of the story.

Sometimes, it's where the comeback begins.

articles.title: Valkyries make history as first-ever women’s sports team to generate over $100 million in revenue
articles.summary: The Golden State Valkyries have set a new standard for successful women’s sports team ownership, grossing the $100 million revenue mark in just their second...
articles.body:
The Golden State Valkyries have set a new standard for successful women's sports team ownership, grossing the $100 million revenue mark in just their second season of existence.

Joe Lacob's ownership group oversaw the rise of the Golden State Warriors into becoming the most valuable NBA franchise, valued at $14.5 billion as of October 2026.

As Lacob entered the WNBA with the Valkyries in 2025, the ownership group has set a new standard for what new women's sports teams can achieve, already considered the most valuable women's sports team in the world. Now, they're proving that with their earnings.

Golden State Valkyries establish themselves as most valuable women's sports team

An ABC news report has revealed that the Valkyries have become the first-ever team in women's sports history to generate over $100 million in revenue over a season.

"The Golden State Valkyries have become the first professional women's sports team to generate $100 million in annual revenue, adding another milestone to a season that has drawn sold-out crowds and helped make the franchise the most valuable team in not just the WNBA, but across all of women's sports."

This does not even factor in the mega-earnings they can have with home Finals games, with the Valkyries confirmed to host Games 1 and 2 at their Chase Centre arena, with Game 5 and 7 also providing boosted earnings if the series goes that far.

The Valkyries will face the Atlanta Dream in the WNBA Finals, with the Dream having one of the WNBA's most popular players in Angel Reese on their roster.

The franchise's ownership model has been hailed since they made their debut in 2025, with many expecting a potential billion-dollar valuation in the next year for the Valkyries, who are currently valued at $850 million. Winning the Finals will definitely put them on that path.

With consistently sold-out home games in the revenue-generating machine that is their home arena at the Chase Centre, the Valkyries have among the brightest futures of all WNBA teams, regardless of the Finals result.

articles.title: Watch broadcaster Emily Austin tell Steve Nash she ran a parody X account on him
articles.summary: Emily Austin is now a popular boxing broadcaster, but she was once an intern for the Brooklyn Nets, running a satirical Twitter account covering Steve Nash....
articles.body:
Boxing broadcaster Emily Austin had been keeping a secret from Steve Nash for years. On Tuesday, October 13, she finally told him to his face, and the camera was rolling when she did.

Austin, 25, crossed paths with the former Brooklyn Nets coach at an NBA on Prime event in New York City. Video she later posted to X shows the two of them together as she comes clean about a social media account she ran in college.

Austin worked as an intern with the Nets while Nash was the team's head coach. During that same stretch, she was also running a satirical Twitter account called "Steve Nash's Burner." The page posted jokes and commentary about the Nets and the man leading them.

The account built a loyal following among Nets fans, and plenty of them eventually figured out that Austin was behind it. Nash never found out. Austin's 'burner" run ended when the platform suspended the account, which she now looks back on as a rough moment from her college years.

Austin described the exchange to Sporting News. She says she started by reminding Nash that she had once interned for the team, since a lot of time had passed.

She then asked him, "Do you remember Steve Nash's Burner account on Twitter? You definitely engaged with it once or twice."

Austin said she told him, "That was me."

According to Austin, Nash broke out laughing and said, "No way, wow OK."

Austin got her start in sports media by interviewing athletes on Instagram Live while she was a student at Hofstra University. She now works as a broadcaster with DAZN and Most Valuable Promotions. Her job takes her to championship boxing, international tennis and basketball, where she interviews some of the biggest names in sports.

Nash is a two time NBA MVP and a Hall of Famer who now works as an analyst for NBA on Prime. He coached the Nets from 2020 to 2022.

He spent those seasons with no idea that one of his own interns was running the account. He knows now.

articles.title: Preocupación en la NBA por la salud de Porzingis, baja indefinida: "No tengo SIDA"
articles.standfirst: "Estoy trabajando con médicos y expertos para determinar cómo recuperar plenamente mi salud (lo antes posible). Sinceramente, cada vez me encuentro mejor"
articles.summary: "Estoy trabajando con médicos y expertos para determinar cómo recuperar plenamente mi salud (lo antes posible). Sinceramente, cada vez me encuentro mejor"
articles.body: Kristaps Porzingis, jugador de los Golden State Warriors que salió de la cantera del Baloncesto Sevilla, permanecerá de baja por tiempo indefinido por un problema de salud de carácter privado. "Estoy trabajando con médicos y expertos para determinar cómo recuperar plenamente mi salud (lo antes posible). Sinceramente, cada vez me encuentro mejor. Sólo tengo que mantener la paciencia; confío en que pronto volveré a sentirme estupendamente", compartió el ala-pívot letón de 31 años y 2,18 m. rompiendo su silencio sobre los problemas de salud que están lastrando su carrera los últimos años. La cadena ESPN publica que Porzingis llamó a Mike Dunleavy, manager general de los Warriors, para informar a la franquicia de que no se incorporaría a la pretemporada del equipo. "Sin duda, resulta frustrante lidiar con problemas de salud que no se pueden identificar con exactitud, sumado a las lesiones que he sufrido a lo largo de mi carrera. Todo esto se ha ido acumulando, pero lograremos superarlo. La salud es lo más importante. Gracias por todo su apoyo", reconoció Porzingis, que todavía no cuenta con el visto bueno médico para poder entrenar, en X (Twitter). Porzingis aprovechó su actividad en redes sociales para desmentir rumores y falsas noticias sobre su salud: "Agradezco a todos los "médicos de internet" que intentan diagnosticarme y ayudar, pero estoy en las mejores manos. Así que todos pueden estar tranquilos: no tengo VIH ni SIDA". Hace dos temporadas Porzingis contrajo un virus de las vías respiratorias superiores. Desde entonces, ha mencionado, aunque sin entrar en detalles, el impacto persistente que esto ha tenido en su salud y en su capacidad para jugar al baloncesto en la NBA de manera constante. La temporada pasada, Porzingis solo pudo disputar 34 partidos, repartidos entre los Atlanta Hawks y los Warriors.

articles.title: La pizarra española toma los banquillos de Europa
articles.standfirst: La Euroliga se rinde al conocimiento, la metodología y la cultura táctica de la escuela española y sus entrenadores. Copan siete de sus 20 banquillos, más de un tercio del total
articles.summary: La Euroliga se rinde al conocimiento, la metodología y la cultura táctica de la escuela española y sus entrenadores. Copan siete de sus 20 banquillos, más de un tercio del total
articles.body: La escuela española toma Europa. La Euroliga dibuja un escenario inédito: siete entrenadores españoles entre los 20 banquillos de la competición, más de un tercio del total. Una conquista silenciosa que confirma que el talento de los técnicos nacionales ya no en una excepción ni una moda, sino una referencia consolidada en el baloncesto continental, donde uno de cada tres banquillos habla español. Pedro Martínez, Xavi Pascual, Pablo Laso, Ibon Navarro, Joan Peñarroya, Álex Mumbrú y Xavier Albert representan una generación de entrenadores formados en una escuela que lleva décadas exportando conocimiento y metodología. Es el resultado de muchos años de trabajo con la Liga Endesa como laboratorio de entrenadores y una cultura táctica muy arraigada han convertido a España en una cantera de técnicos de primer nivel. Estos son los retos que afrontan los entrenadores españoles en esta próxima Euroliga. El gran escaparate es el Real Madrid y, con él, uno de los mayores desafíos de la carrera de Pedro Martínez. El técnico catalán ha aterrizado en el banquillo blanco después de una trayectoria de casi cuatro décadas en los banquillos y con 34 temporadas y 1.103 partidos dirigidos en la Liga Endesa. Llega, además, después de conquistar la pasada temporada la Liga Endesa y la Supercopa con el Valencia Basket, y con el aval de dos Ligas, dos Supercopas y una Copa Korac en su palmarés. Su fichaje por tres temporadas supone la apuesta firme del Madrid por un entrenador español de enorme experiencia para recuperar el rumbo de una sección que viene de quedarse en blanco 16 años después. En el club blanco no basta con competir: hay que ganar. Y tras una temporada sin títulos, el margen de exigencia se dispara. El objetivo de Pedro Martínez debe ser construir un equipo reconocible, intenso y ambicioso, capaz de pelear desde el primer día por la Liga y la Copa, pero con la Euroliga como gran termómetro de su proyecto. Y ganar títulos, claro. En Oriente Medio, a miles de kilómetros, Xavi Pascual vuelve a colocarse en el centro del mapa baloncestístico europeo al frente del Dubai Basketball. El técnico de Gavà, campeón de la Euroliga en 2010 con el Barcelona y uno de los entrenadores españoles con mayor recorrido internacional, ha asumido el mando de un proyecto que quiere dejar de ser una novedad para convertirse en una realidad de la élite continental. Firma hasta 2029 y llega a los Emiratos Árabes después de haber dirigido al Barça, Panathinaikos y Zenit, acumulando una experiencia de primer nivel clave para el salto de ambición del club. Dubái ya no se conforma con participar: quiere competir y mirar de frente a los grandes. Después de conquistar la ABA League en su primera temporada y de un debut histórico en la Euroliga, el objetivo pasa por consolidarse entre los mejores y aspirar incluso a la Final Four. Para ello, Pascual deberá dotar de identidad, orden y exigencia a un equipo construido para crecer a gran velocidad. Su experiencia en escenarios de máxima presión será el gran argumento para acelerar ese proceso. El proyecto emiratí pone el músculo económico; Pascual, el conocimiento y la cultura competitiva necesarios para convertir una ambición en un candidato de verdad. En su segunda campaña en Estambul, Pablo Laso afronta el reto de devolver al Anadolu Efes a la élite europea. Tras llegar en diciembre y asumir un equipo lastrado por las lesiones, el técnico apenas tuvo margen para implantar sus ideas y el conjunto turco acabó penúltimo en la Euroliga. El club mantiene su confianza en él y le ha entregado ahora una profunda reconstrucción, con un verano completo para diseñar el proyecto a su medida. El cambio de ciclo está marcado por la salida de Shane Larkin al Fenerbahçe y por la grave lesión de Mike James, su fichaje estrella, que será baja toda la temporada y ha sido reemplazado por Cameron Payne. No tendrá al máximo anotador histórico de la Euroliga, pero sí otros refuerzos como Bruno Fernando, Matthew Strazel, Santi Yusta o Dario Saric. El objetivo es recuperar la identidad competitiva de un equipo que conquistó dos Euroligas consecutivas en 2021 y 2022 y que, con Laso al frente desde el inicio, un entrenador ganador, aspira de nuevo a pelear por todo. En Belgrado, Ibon Navarro afronta el mayor desafío de su carrera al frente de un Estrella Roja que busca dar un paso adelante en la Euroliga. El técnico vitoriano ha llegado a Serbia después de cerrar el ciclo más exitoso de la historia del Unicaja, con siete títulos en cuatro temporadas y media, y con el aval de haberse convertido en uno de los entrenadores españoles de referencia. El salto a la Euroliga supone también cumplir una aspiración de Navarro: medirse de tú a tú con los grandes de Europa y demostrar su valía en el máximo escenario continental. El reto no será menor. El Estrella Roja se quedó la pasada temporada a las puertas de los playoffs y ha reforzado el proyecto con Johnathan Motley, Chris Jones y David Krämer, además de mantener piezas importantes como Jared Butler, Nikola Kalinic u Ognjen Dobric. La misión de Navarro será convertir ese talento en un equipo reconocible, físico y competitivo, capaz de hacerse fuerte en el infierno de Belgrado y, sobre todo, de instalar al Estrella Roja de forma estable entre los mejores de Europa. En su segunda campaña al frente del Partizan, Joan Peñarroya afronta el reto de convertir en proyecto estable lo que comenzó como una misión de urgencia. El técnico catalán llegó a Belgrado en diciembre en un escenario especialmente exigente para suceder al mito Zeljko Obradovic, y acabó cerrando el curso con una espectacular reacción, incluida una racha de seis victorias consecutivas en la Euroliga. Ahora ha dispuesto de un verano completo para construir su Partizan, con una plantilla muy renovada y hasta ocho salidas, entre ellas las de Nick Calathes, Shake Milton, Bruno Fernando o Sterling Brown. La exigencia en Belgrado es máxima. El Partizan encadena tres temporadas sin terminar entre los diez primeros de la Euroliga y necesita recuperar cuanto antes su condición de gigante continental. Peñarroya contará para ello con las incorporaciones de Kevarrius Hayes, Lamar Stevens, Luca Vildoza o Ethan Thompson, entre otros. Su objetivo es devolver al Partizan a los playoffs de la Euroliga y demostrar que su crecimiento en los banquillos tiene recorrido en uno de los escenarios más calientes y exigentes del baloncesto europeo. En Bolonia comienza una nueva etapa para Álex Mumbrú, que afronta su estreno en la Virtus con el aval de haberse proclamado campeón del mundo y de Europa al frente de Alemania y con el desafío de trasladar ese conocimiento al día a día de un club de máxima exigencia. La Virtus busca dar un salto competitivo en una Euroliga cada vez más exigente y el técnico catalán intentará dotar de identidad a un proyecto renovado, con un equipo profundo y versátil. Los mimbres invitan al optimismo. Mumbrú contará con una mezcla de jugadores experimentados como Daniel Hackett y Derrick Alston Jr. y jóvenes con margen de crecimiento, además de incorporaciones como Tommaso Baldasso, Riccardo Casarin, Rasheed Bello o Kevin Kokila. El objetivo debe ser devolver a la Virtus a la pelea por los puestos altos de la Euroliga. Mumbrú tiene la oportunidad de consolidarse en la élite de los banquillos y convertir a la histórica Virtus en un equipo reconocible, competitivo y preparado para volver a mirar a la cara a los grandes de Europa. Xavi Albert afronta el mayor reto de su carrera al tomar el relevo de Pedro Martínez en un Valencia Basket que viene de conquistar Liga Endesa y Supercopa, pero que ha perdido a piezas fundamentales como Jean Montero, Brancou Badio, Braxton Key, Darius Thompson o Jaime Pradilla. El club ha respondido con una renovación ambiciosa, liderada por TJ Shorts, Nikola Mirotic y Armoni Brooks, además de jugadores como Dylan Osetkowski, Elias Valtonen, Gonzalo Corbalán o Mario Saint-Supéry. Albert, que conoce perfectamente la casa, tendrá que ensamblar todas esas piezas y mantener la competitividad de un campeón. La Euroliga será su gran examen. El Valencia es un grande del baloncesto español y europeo y, tras alcanzar la Final Four, ya no puede conformarse con competir: debe aspirar a estar entre los mejores. Para Albert, debutante como primer entrenador, supone una oportunidad extraordinaria para demostrar su capacidad, pero también la responsabilidad de mantener al equipo en la élite y gestionar la inevitable comparación con Pedro Martínez. Su gran desafío será conseguir que el nuevo proyecto mantenga las mismas ambición y exigencia que han convertido al Valencia en un referente europeo.

articles.summary: Le preguntan directamente a Delonte West: "¿Tuviste relaciones sexuales con la madre de LeBron James?"
articles.body: Delonte West ofrece una respuesta enigmática tras ser cuestionado sobre su supuesta relación sentimental con Gloria James, la madre de LeBron James, cuando ambos eran compañeros de equipo. "Delonte West, ¿tuviste relaciones sexuales con la madre de LeBron James?", le pregúntó directamente el cómico Supa Hot Fire al alma más atormentada de la NBA. La respuesta del exjugador de 43 años fue que "un caballero nunca cuenta esas cosas". El pasado mes de marzo Delonte West reveló que llevaba 100 días sobrio. Y hace un mes trascendió que ese periodo ya alcanzaba los 10 meses. West tiene previsto enfrentarse a Michael Beasley, también exjugador de la NBA, en un combate de boxeo durante el evento 'Brand Risk 16' organizado por Adin Ross en Miami. El rumor del supuesto romance de Delonte West con la madre de LeBron James surgió durante los playoffs de la NBA de 2010, cuando los Cleveland Cavaliers fueron eliminados por los Boston Celtics en segunda ronda. "Adondequiera que voy, la primera pregunta es: "No me digas que hiciste eso. Para empezar, algo así nunca ocurrió. No sé de dónde sacaron eso. Es terrible que la gente intente desprestigiar a una mujer negra fuerte como ella. Es terrible en muchos sentidos", aclaró Delonte West en 2012. Delonte West desveló en agosto que en sus momentos más difíciles LeBron y Gloria estuvieron pendientes de él y de su madre para asegurarse de que lograran sobrellevar la situación. "Muchos de los compañeros con los que jugué... LeBron es mi amigo, y su familia ha llamado... Sí, él llama a mi madre constantemente para asegurarse de que estoy bien. La señora James, la señora Gloria, llama a mi madre para ver cómo sigue todo. Me dice: "Dile a mi hijo que lo he visto. ¡Más le vale enderezar el rumbo!", contó en 'N3on'.
